original_source_text: We present MTIA 300, Meta’s first AI training chip optimized for Deep Learning Recommendation Models (DLRMs). Unlike GenAI training, DLRM training requires modest FLOPS but large memory, high network bandwidth, and frequent collective communication; this combination often leads to low accelerator utilization. MTIA 300 addresses these challenges with three key innovations: (1) built-in NIC chiplets with 12×800 Gbps RDMA NICs to ensure high network performance and eliminate PCIe overhead; (2) dedicated message engines for collective offloading, delivering throughput comparable to compute engines while using only one-third of the chip area; and (3) near- memory compute, placing message engines close to HBM, cache, and I/O, with specialized hardware to accelerate reduction- based collectives such as ReduceScatter. While motivated by DLRMs, these broadly applicable design principles carry over to subsequent MTIA generations (MTIA 400, 450, and 500) optimized for GenAI models. To our knowledge, MTIA 300 is the first accelerator with built-in NIC chiplets and general-purpose collective offloading engines, enabling efficient scale-up and scale- out communication. Furthermore, while MTIA 300’s combination of moderate FLOPS and higher HBM bandwidth and capacity was initially optimized for training DLRMs, these characteristics make it effective for GenAI inference. Performance evaluation shows that MTIA 300 is competitive with same-generation GPUs while offering cost advantages.

record_under_review.evidence_span: Sections II and IV describe integrated RDMA NIC chiplets, dedicated message engines, near-memory reductions, and HCCL software. Section V.D.1 reports 3.9x communication performance versus H100 for a roughly 150B-parameter DLRM using 40 accelerators and local batch 6144. Table IV reports normalized Perf/TCO separately. Section V.B reports an H100/NCCL advantage for small messages; Section VI discusses numerical, datatype, runtime, and training-batch limitations.
record_under_review.hardware_or_process_assumptions: Table I: 1.9 GHz, 216 GB HBM3E, 912 W TDP (667 W typical), compute chiplet 25.6 x 31.4 mm, two network chiplets each 25.6 x 9.3 mm. Section II: 12 x 800 Gbps RDMA NICs and 16 message engines. Process node not established in extracted sections; TDP is not measured workload energy.
record_under_review.limits: Author-reported evaluation, not independent replication. Communication speedup and Perf/TCO are distinct; neither establishes universal end-to-end speedup. Cost-accounting inputs and amortization assumptions were not found in the extracted evaluation and remain unresolved. Small-message collectives favor H100/NCCL; compute-heavy workloads, numerical parity, unsupported datatypes, eager overhead, and convergence/batch tradeoffs limit generality. Exact article-only 940 GB/s and less-than-0.5% figures remain supplemental, not paper-verified metrics.
record_under_review.method_or_artifact: MTIA 300 co-designs compute, integrated network chiplets, dedicated message engines, near-memory collective reduction, and the HCCL communication library; collectives are compiled into autonomous dependency graphs rather than launched as compute-grid kernels.
metrics: 3.9x communication performance relative to H100: 40 accelerators, local batch 6144, approximately 150B-parameter DLRM (V.D.1)

record_under_review.problem: Recommendation-model training is communication-bound because embedding tables contain most model parameters and hybrid parallelism generates frequent AllReduce, AllToAll, and AllGather operations that compete with computation on GPU resources.

supplemental_sources.limits: Article-only exact figures such as 940 GB/s and less than 0.5% are not promoted into the paper-derived metric list.
